claims.text: What the image looks like Buzzword: apple-core lesion (barium / CT colon) = colorectal carcinoma
claims.quote: Apple-core lesion Barium / CT colon Colorectal carcinoma

claims.text: Upper GI / barium enema: apple-core lesion → colorectal carcinoma
Barium swallow: apple-core annular narrowing → esophageal/colonic carcinoma
Aspects (abnormal in red) Diagnosis: colonoscopic biopsy; CT to evaluate the extent of tumor growth and spread
claims.quote: Colonoscopic biopsy CT to evaluate extent of tumor growth and spread

claims.text: Barium enema (particularly double-contrast) can detect many lesions but is somewhat less accurate than colonoscopy and is not acceptable follow-up to a positive fecal occult blood or DNA test
claims.quote: Barium enema radiograph, particularly a double-contrast study, can detect many lesions but is somewhat less accurate than colonoscopy and is not acceptable as follow-up to a positive fecal occult blood test or positive DNA test.

claims.text: Positive fecal occult blood or fecal DNA test, or a lesion seen on sigmoidoscopy or imaging → colonoscopy; all lesions should be completely removed for histology
claims.quote: Patients with positive fecal occult blood tests or positive fecal DNA tests require colonoscopy, as do those with lesions seen during sigmoidoscopy or an imaging study. All lesions should be completely removed for histologic examination.

claims.text: Once diagnosed: staging CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis and routine labs to seek metastases; refer to a colorectal cancer specialist
claims.quote: Once cancer is diagnosed, patients should undergo complete imaging staging with CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and routine laboratory tests to seek metastatic disease. Referral should be made to a specialist in the treatment of colorectal cancer (eg, colorectal surgeon, surgical oncologist).

claims.text: CEA is routinely obtained at the initial evaluation but is neither sensitive nor specific, so it is not recommended for screening; it is routinely monitored after treatment
claims.quote: CEA level is routinely obtained as part of the initial evaluation for CRC, but this test is neither sensitive nor specific and therefore is not recommended for screening purposes. CEA levels are routinely monitored following treatment.

claims.text: Causes Most often arises by transformation within adenomatous polyps; approximately 80% sporadic, 20% with an inheritable component; many genetic syndromes predispose (eg, familial adenomatous polyposis)
claims.quote: Colorectal cancer (CRC) most often occurs as transformation within adenomatous polyps. Approximately 80% of cases are sporadic, and 20% have an inheritable component. Many genetic syndromes predispose to CRC: Familial adenomatous polyposis

claims.text: High-incidence populations eat low-fiber diets high in animal protein, fat and refined carbohydrates; the exact mechanism is unknown
claims.quote: Patients in populations with a high incidence of CRC eat low-fiber diets that are high in animal protein, fat, and refined carbohydrates. Carcinogens may be ingested in the diet but are more likely produced by bacterial action on dietary substances or biliary or intestinal secretions. The exact mechanism is unknown.

claims.text: Spreads by direct extension through the bowel wall, hematogenous metastasis, regional lymph node metastasis and perineural spread
claims.quote: CRC spreads by direct extension through the bowel wall, hematogenous metastasis, regional lymph node metastasis, and perineural spread.

claims.text: Symptoms Right-sided lesions usually manifest with bleeding and anemia; left-sided lesions usually with obstructive symptoms (eg, colicky abdominal pain)
claims.quote: Right-sided lesions usually manifest with bleeding and anemia; left-sided lesions usually manifest with obstructive symptoms (eg, colicky abdominal pain).

claims.text: Right colon: large caliber, thin wall, liquid contents, so obstruction is a late event; bleeding is usually occult; fatigue and weakness from severe anemia may be the only complaints
claims.quote: The right colon has a large caliber and a thin wall and its contents are liquid; thus, obstruction is a late event. Bleeding is usually occult. Fatigue and weakness caused by severe anemia may be the only complaints, and tumors are often asymptomatic and are detected only when colonoscopy or cross-sectional imaging is done for another reason.

claims.text: Left colon: smaller lumen, semisolid feces, so cancer tends to obstruct earlier; partial obstruction with colicky pain or complete obstruction may be the first sign; the stool may be streaked or mixed with blood
claims.quote: The left colon has a smaller lumen, the feces are semisolid, and cancer tends to cause obstruction earlier than in the right colon. Partial obstruction with colicky abdominal pain or complete obstruction may be the initial manifestation. The stool may be streaked or mixed with blood.

claims.text: Rectal cancer: most common first symptom is bleeding with defecation; whenever rectal bleeding occurs, even with obvious hemorrhoids or known diverticular disease, coexisting cancer must be ruled out
claims.quote: In rectal cancer, the most common initial symptom is bleeding with defecation. Whenever rectal bleeding occurs, even with obvious hemorrhoids or known diverticular disease, coexisting cancer must be ruled out.

claims.text: Treatment and next step Surgical resection is the mainstay of curative treatment: removal of the tumor-bearing segment with its regional lymphatic drainage
claims.quote: Surgical resection is the mainstay for curative-intent treatment of CRC. Resection consists of removal of the anatomic segment of the large intestine harboring the tumor along with its regional lymphatic drainage.

claims.text: Colon cancer: postoperative chemotherapy for stage III (lymph node-positive) or high-risk stage II disease
claims.quote: In colon cancer, postoperative chemotherapy is indicated for patients with stage III disease (lymph node-positive) or patients with high-risk stage II disease (lymph node-negative but high-risk features seen on pathology such as lymphovascular invasion)

claims.text: Rectal cancer: in general, locally advanced disease (T3 or T4) or suspected nodal disease gets chemotherapy and chemoradiation before surgery
claims.quote: In general, patients with locally advanced disease (T3 or T4) or who are suspected of having nodal disease will receive both chemotherapy and chemoradiation prior to surgical resection.

claims.text: After curative resection: surveillance colonoscopy at 1 year, a second 3 years later if no polyps or tumors are found, then every 5 years
claims.quote: After curative surgical resection of colorectal cancer, surveillance colonoscopy should be done 1 year after surgery or after the clearing preoperative colonoscopy (6). A second surveillance colonoscopy should be done 3 years after the 1-year surveillance colonoscopy if no polyps or tumors are found. Thereafter, surveillance colonoscopy should be done every 5 years.
